name: Label and select pods
objective: CKAD core: label and annotate objects, and target them with equality + set-based selectors. Add/overwrite/remove labels, bulk-label via a selector, set-based matching, matchExpressions selectors, annotations, and a selector-mismatch diagnose-fix. Graded exactly.

questions.title: Add a label
questions.teach:
`kubectl label <kind>/<name> key=value` attaches a label (key/value metadata used for selecting and grouping objects).

**Gotcha:** labelling an existing key without `--overwrite` fails — add fails loudly rather than clobbering.
questions.prompt:
In `labels-learn`, add the label `env=prod` to pod `frontend`.

Target: pod `frontend` has label `env=prod`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod frontend env=prod
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod frontend --show-labels
questions.eli5:
Imagine every pod is a kid at summer camp, and a **label** is a sticker you press onto a kid's name tag. Each sticker is just a short note like `env=prod` ("this kid is in the Prod group"). Stickers don't change the kid at all — they're just a way for the counsellors to find and group kids later ("everyone with the Prod sticker, line up!").

To stick one on, you point at the kid by name and say what the sticker says:

```
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod frontend env=prod
```

That reads as: "In the `labels-learn` camp, on the pod named `frontend`, add the sticker `env=prod`."

The one surprising rule: if that kid **already** has an `env` sticker, Kubernetes won't quietly peel it off and slap on a new one. It stops and complains loudly instead — it refuses to clobber what's there unless you explicitly say "yes, overwrite it" (with `--overwrite`, which is the next lesson).

**Watch out:**

- **Adding a label whose key already exists FAILS** (with an error) unless you pass `--overwrite`. It won't silently replace it — that's on purpose, so you don't lose data by accident.
- The format is `key=value` with an **equals sign** — `env=prod`, not `env prod` or `env:prod`.
- Don't forget the **namespace** (`-n labels-learn`), or kubectl looks in the wrong place and says the pod isn't found.
- Labels are for **grouping and selecting**; check them with `--show-labels`.
questions.deepDive:
## Adding labels — full rundown

### What a label is
A **label** is a `key=value` pair in an object's `metadata.labels`. Labels are the primary mechanism for **identifying and grouping** objects: Services, ReplicaSets, Deployments, `kubectl -l`, and network policies all *select* on labels. They are indexed and meant to be queried.

### The command
```bash
kubectl label <kind>/<name> key=value
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod frontend env=prod      # add env=prod to pod frontend
```
- `<kind>/<name>` or `<kind> <name>` both work (`pod/frontend` == `pod frontend`).
- Add multiple at once: `kubectl label pod frontend env=prod tier=web`.

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod frontend --show-labels
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod frontend -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'; echo
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -L env           # show env label as its own column
```

### Add / overwrite / remove at a glance
| Action | Command |
|---|---|
| Add a new label | `kubectl label pod frontend env=prod` |
| Overwrite existing key | `kubectl label --overwrite pod frontend env=stage` |
| Remove a label | `kubectl label pod frontend env-` *(trailing dash)* |
| Label many at once | `kubectl label pods -l app=shop tier=web` |

### Label syntax rules (what's valid)
| Part | Constraint |
|---|---|
| Key name | ≤ 63 chars, `[a-z0-9A-Z]` start/end, may contain `-_.` |
| Key prefix (optional) | `dns-subdomain/` before name, e.g. `example.com/team` |
| Value | ≤ 63 chars, same charset, **may be empty** |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Re-labelling an existing key without `--overwrite` errors out** — `error: 'env' already has a value (dev), and --overwrite is false`. This is deliberate: it protects against silent clobbering.
- Use `key=value` (equals), not `key:value` (that's YAML, not the CLI form).
- Specify the **namespace** (`-n`) — labels are namespaced along with their object.
- Changing a pod's labels can **add or remove it from a Service/ReplicaSet** instantly — a controller may adopt or orphan it.
- A label **value can be empty** (`key=`) but the key cannot.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod frontend env=prod          # add
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod frontend env=qa # change
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod frontend env-               # remove
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod frontend --show-labels        # verify
```

questions.title: Overwrite and remove a label
questions.teach:
Change an existing label with `kubectl label --overwrite key=newvalue`; remove one with `kubectl label <obj> key-` (trailing dash).

**Gotcha:** without `--overwrite`, relabelling an existing key errors; `key-` (not `key=`) is how you delete a label.
questions.prompt:
Pod `legacy` in `labels-learn` has labels `env=dev` and `deprecated=true`. **Overwrite** `env` to `prod`, and **remove** the `deprecated` label.

Target: pod `legacy` has `env=prod` and no `deprecated` label.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod` and `kubectl -n labels-learn label pod legacy deprecated-`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod legacy deprecated-
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod legacy --show-labels
questions.eli5:
Keep the name-tag-sticker picture from before. Now a kid named `legacy` already has two stickers: `env=dev` and `deprecated=true`. Your job is to **change one** and **peel one off**.

Changing a sticker: because Kubernetes refuses to quietly cover up an existing sticker, you must explicitly say "yes, replace it" with `--overwrite`:

```
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod
```

That swaps the `env` sticker from `dev` to `prod`.

Peeling a sticker off is a special little move: you type the key followed by a **minus sign** and *nothing after it* — that trailing dash means "remove."

```
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod legacy deprecated-
```

Notice: `deprecated-` (dash), **not** `deprecated=` (equals). `deprecated=` would try to set an empty value, which is not the same as removing the sticker entirely.

**Watch out:**

- **To change an existing label you MUST pass `--overwrite`** — without it, Kubernetes errors instead of clobbering.
- **To delete a label use `key-` (trailing dash), NOT `key=`.** `key=` sets an empty value; `key-` removes the label entirely.
- You can do both in one go or as two commands — the dash-remove doesn't need `--overwrite`.
- Removing a label can **drop the pod out of a Service or controller** that was selecting on it — grouping is live.
- Double-check with `--show-labels` so you can see the final sticker set.
questions.deepDive:
## Overwriting & removing labels — full rundown

### Mental model
`kubectl label` is **not idempotent for an existing key**. Setting a key that already exists is treated as a *conflict* unless you opt in with `--overwrite`. Removal is a distinct syntax: `key-` (trailing dash), which is **not** the same as `key=` (empty value).

### Overwrite an existing label
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod
```
Without `--overwrite`:
```
error: 'env' already has a value (dev), and --overwrite is false
```

### Remove a label
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod legacy deprecated-      # trailing dash = delete
```

### `key-` vs `key=` — the critical distinction
| Form | Meaning | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `key=value` | set to a value (new key) | adds `key=value` |
| `key=` | set to **empty string** | `key: ""` still present |
| `key-` | **remove** the label | key gone from `metadata.labels` |
| `--overwrite key=value` | replace existing value | `key=value` |

### Doing both in one invocation
```bash
# one command: overwrite env, delete deprecated
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod deprecated-
```
`--overwrite` is only needed for the *set* part; the `deprecated-` removal works without it.

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod legacy --show-labels
# env=prod  (no deprecated= anywhere)
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod legacy -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`--overwrite` is mandatory** to change a key that already has a value — otherwise the command fails loudly.
- **Delete uses `key-`, not `key=`.** `key=` leaves the label present with an empty value; graders checking "no X label" will still see it.
- `--overwrite` is harmless when adding a brand-new key, so you can keep it on by habit — but removal (`key-`) is a separate token.
- Mutating labels is **live**: removing a selector label can instantly orphan the pod from its Service/ReplicaSet (and a bare pod may be deleted if a ReplicaSet no longer counts it).
- You cannot "rename" a label — remove the old key and add the new one.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod   # change value
kubectl -n labels-learn label pod legacy deprecated-            # delete label
kubectl -n labels-learn label --overwrite pod legacy env=prod deprecated-  # both
kubectl -n labels-learn get pod legacy --show-labels            # verify
```

questions.title: Bulk-label via a selector
questions.teach:
Label many objects at once by targeting them with `-l <selector>`: `kubectl label pods -l app=shop tier=web` labels every pod matching `app=shop`.

**Gotcha:** `-l` on `kubectl label` selects *which* objects to label — it doesn't set that label.
questions.prompt:
In `labels-learn`, add the label `tier=web` to **all** pods that match `app=shop` (there are two), in one command.

Target: every `app=shop` pod has `tier=web`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l app=shop tier=web
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -l app=shop --show-labels

verification.description: all app=shop pods now have tier=web

questions.eli5:
Picture a classroom full of kids (pods). You want to put a `tier=web` sticker on **every kid who already wears the `app=shop` badge** — maybe twenty of them, maybe two — without walking up to each one by name.

The trick is `-l` (the "which kids?" filter). It answers *who* gets touched, while the plain `key=value` at the end says *what sticker* to add:

```
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l app=shop tier=web
```

Read it left to right: "label pods — **but only the ones matching `app=shop`** (that's the `-l` part) — with the sticker `tier=web`." Everyone wearing the shop badge gets the web sticker in one command; nobody else is touched.

The part that trips people up: `-l app=shop` is **not** a sticker being applied. It's the *search filter* for choosing the crowd. The sticker being applied is the bare `tier=web` at the very end, with no `-l` in front of it.

**Watch out:**

- **`-l <selector>` chooses WHICH objects to label — it does not set that label.** Only the bare `key=value` (no `-l`) is applied.
- If the selector matches **zero** pods, kubectl labels nothing and may say "no resources found" — it won't error dramatically, so verify.
- You must name the **resource type** (`pods`) because you're selecting a whole group, not one named object.
- Confirm the result with `kubectl get pods -l app=shop --show-labels` to see every matched pod now carries `tier=web`.
- Don't forget the namespace (`-n labels-learn`).
questions.deepDive:
## Bulk-labelling via a selector — full rundown

### Mental model
`kubectl label` has two distinct roles for `key=value`-ish arguments:
- **`-l <selector>`** → *filters which objects* the command operates on (the audience).
- **bare `key=value`** → *the label to write* onto each matched object (the action).

They are not the same thing. `-l app=shop` selects; `tier=web` sets.

### The command
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l app=shop tier=web
#                           │     │             └ label APPLIED to each match
#                           │     └ selector: WHICH pods
#                           └ resource type (plural: a group)
```

### Equality selectors you can filter on
| Selector | Matches |
|---|---|
| `app=shop` | objects with `app` exactly `shop` |
| `app!=shop` | objects whose `app` is not `shop` (incl. where present but different) |
| `app=shop,tier=web` | **both** (comma = AND) |

### Applying multiple labels to the selected set
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l app=shop tier=web zone=a
```

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -l app=shop --show-labels   # every match now has tier=web
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -L app -L tier              # columns for app + tier
```

### `--all` vs `-l`
```bash
kubectl label pods --all debug=true      # every pod in the namespace
kubectl label pods -l app=shop debug=true # only the app=shop subset
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`-l` picks targets; it does not set a label.** The label to add is the bare `key=value` argument — a frequent mix-up.
- **Zero matches = nothing labelled.** kubectl reports "No resources found"; it does not fail hard, so always verify afterward.
- Use the **plural/collective resource name** (`pods`) with `-l`; you're operating on a set, not a single named object.
- Combine with `--overwrite` if the selected pods may already carry the key you're setting.
- `-l` on `kubectl label` is the *same* selector syntax used by `kubectl get -l`, Services, and controllers — one grammar everywhere.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l app=shop tier=web      # bulk add to a subset
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods --all audited=true        # all pods in ns
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -l app=shop --show-labels   # verify
```

questions.title: Set-based selector targeting
questions.teach:
Set-based selectors match against a set of values: `-l 'release in (beta,rc)'`, `notin (...)`, or `key`/`!key` (exists / not-exists). Use them to target a subset.

**Gotcha:** quote the selector in the shell; equality (`=`,`!=`) and set-based (`in`,`notin`) can be combined with commas.
questions.prompt:
In `labels-learn`, add `canary=yes` to every pod whose `release` is **in (beta, rc)** — using a set-based selector. The `release=stable` pod must NOT get it.

Target: `rel-beta` and `rel-rc` have `canary=yes`; `rel-stable` does not.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l 'release in (beta,rc)' canary=yes
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -L release -L canary
questions.eli5:
So far your filters have been "must equal exactly this." But sometimes you want "anybody whose badge is one of *these* few options." That's a **set-based selector** — it matches against a little list of allowed values.

Imagine pods wearing `release` badges: one says `beta`, one says `rc`, one says `stable`. You want to sticker `canary=yes` onto the `beta` and `rc` ones, but **leave `stable` alone**. Instead of running two separate commands, you say "release is *in* this list":

```
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l 'release in (beta,rc)' canary=yes
```

`release in (beta,rc)` means "pick pods whose `release` value is either `beta` or `rc`." The `stable` pod doesn't match, so it stays untouched.

There's a whole family of these: `notin (...)` ("not any of these"), `release` by itself ("has a release badge at all"), and `!release` ("has no release badge").

**Watch out:**

- **Quote the selector** in the shell — `'release in (beta,rc)'` — because the parentheses and spaces confuse bash otherwise.
- The sticker applied is still the **bare `canary=yes`** at the end; the `-l '...'` only chooses who.
- You can **mix** equality and set-based with commas: `-l 'app=shop,release in (beta,rc)'` (comma = AND).
- `key` alone = "exists"; `!key` = "does not exist" — these check presence, not value.
- Verify carefully that `stable` did **not** get the sticker: `kubectl get pods -L release -L canary`.
questions.deepDive:
## Set-based selectors — full rundown

### Mental model
Kubernetes has **two selector grammars**:
- **Equality-based**: `=`, `==`, `!=` — compare a key to one value.
- **Set-based**: `in`, `notin`, `exists` (`key`), `!key` — test membership in a set or mere presence.

`kubectl -l` accepts both, and you can combine them with commas (AND). Set-based is what `matchExpressions` encodes in object specs.

### The command
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn label pods -l 'release in (beta,rc)' canary=yes
```
Only pods whose `release` is `beta` **or** `rc` get `canary=yes`; `release=stable` is skipped.

### Operator table
| Selector (CLI) | Meaning | matchExpressions equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `release in (beta,rc)` | value is one of the set | `{key: release, operator: In, values: [beta, rc]}` |
| `release notin (stable)` | value is **not** in the set | `{operator: NotIn, values: [stable]}` |
| `release` | key **exists** (any value) | `{operator: Exists}` |
| `!release` | key does **not** exist | `{operator: DoesNotExist}` |
| `env=prod` | equality | `{key: env, operator: In, values: [prod]}` (via matchLabels) |
| `env!=prod` | inequality | `{operator: NotIn, values: [prod]}` |

### Combining (comma = AND)
```bash
kubectl -l 'app=shop,release in (beta,rc)' ...       # equality AND set-based
kubectl -l 'release,!canary' ...                     # has release, lacks canary
```

### Shell quoting
Always single-quote set-based selectors — `(`, `)`, spaces and `!` are shell-special:
```bash
kubectl -l 'release in (beta,rc)'      # correct
kubectl -l release in (beta,rc)        # bash error: syntax near '('
```
Note: there is **no space** required after the comma inside the set — `(beta,rc)` and `(beta, rc)` both parse.

### Verifying a selective result
```bash
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -L release -L canary
# rel-beta   beta   yes
# rel-rc     rc     yes
# rel-stable stable        <-- canary column empty: correct
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Quote the whole selector** in the shell, or parentheses break the command.
- `-l` chooses targets; the **bare `canary=yes`** is what gets written — same rule as equality bulk-labelling.
- **Exists vs value**: `release` tests *presence*, not a specific value; don't confuse with `release=` (empty value equality).
- `notin` matches objects **without** the key too (they trivially aren't in the set) — be explicit if that matters.
- Set-based selectors are the CLI face of **`matchExpressions`**; Services only support equality `matchLabels`-style selectors in their `spec.selector`, while Deployments/ReplicaSets support `matchExpressions`.
- Verify the *excluded* object stayed clean, not just that the included ones got labelled.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -l 'release in (beta,rc)'  label pods canary=yes    # in
kubectl -l 'release notin (stable)' get pods                # notin
kubectl -l 'release'   get pods                             # exists
kubectl -l '!canary'   get pods                             # does not exist
kubectl -n labels-learn get pods -L release -L canary       # verify columns
```
